name: Breast developers (pills and creams)

lead: These products are sold as pills or creams claimed to increase breast size, aiming for a fuller bust profile without surgery. They are marketed as natural.

Their ingredients are typically plant or fungal extracts such as fenugreek, dong quai and Pueraria mirifica, many described as estrogen mimics. Reviews report that no randomised, blinded, fully controlled trials have tested them.

paras: Taken as capsules or applied as creams over weeks to months, as the labels describe.
Concerns include possible breast cancer risk from estrogen-like compounds, liver effects with kava and interactions with drugs; the FTC and FDA have acted against makers for fraud.

chain: Herbal estrogen-like ingredients taken or applied
angle.text: Sellers claim the ingredients enlarge breast tissue. Users take capsules or apply creams hoping for volume without surgery.

lead: Breast developers are supplements and creams sold to enlarge the breasts without surgery, marketed as natural and risk free [1]. People use them hoping for a fuller bust.

Most contain plant or fungal ingredients such as black cohosh, dong quai, fenugreek, hops, kava and Pueraria mirifica, many with claimed estrogen-mimicking compounds [1]. Wikipedia reports no randomised, blinded, fully controlled trials and that some companies have faked testimonials [1].

In the US they are sold under generally-recognised-as-safe rules and are not approved for any medical use; the FTC and FDA have acted against manufacturers, and the Mayo Clinic warns of drug interactions [1]. A separate Wikipedia article calls the Mark Eden bust developer a fraudulently marketed device [2].
infobox: FTC and FDA actions against some makers

paras: Zearalenone, a mold-produced estrogen mimic, may stimulate breast cancer cell growth and reduce fertility; kava may cause liver damage; dong quai is among ingredients described as carcinogenic; black cohosh showed no estrogenic effect in testing [1].
Weight gain adds fat in varying amounts near the breasts, and a 2007 paper examined the Brava external expander [2].
